grammar_topic: word order in questions; present simple
title: Five Minutes to Decide
body: At the speed-dating event, every couple has exactly five minutes together before a bell rings. 'What do you do at the weekends?' Aziz asks the woman across the table. 'I paint,' she says, 'and I never miss my Sunday run.' She seems confident and funny, and Aziz likes her immediately. 'Where do you usually go on holiday?' she asks him back. 'I don't travel much,' he admits, 'but I love cooking for my friends.' The bell rings before they finish talking, and Aziz moves to the next table, disappointed. Ten conversations later, he still thinks about her answers. At the end of the evening, the organizer reads out the matches. 'Table four and table nine — you both chose each other!' Aziz laughs with relief; table nine was exactly the woman with the Sunday run. He finally has her number, and this time there's no bell to stop the conversation.

words.context: She seems confident and funny.
The organizer reads out the matches.
Aziz laughs with relief.
'I don't travel much,' he admits.
Aziz moves to the next table, disappointed.
You both chose each other — a match!

grammar_topic: present simple; present continuous
title: The Renovation Show
body: Every Friday, millions of people watch 'Home Makeover' on television. The show usually follows the same pattern: a family lives in an old, tired house, and two designers arrive with big plans. This week, the Karimov family is standing in their garden, watching workers carry furniture out of the house. 'We're renovating the kitchen and the bathroom,' explains the lead designer, 'and we're also painting every room a different colour.' The family doesn't usually spend much money on their home, so they're a little nervous. Right now, one worker is knocking down an old wall, while another is measuring the new kitchen island. By the end of the episode, the house always looks completely different. The Karimovs are currently living with relatives, but they're counting the days until they can move back. 'I can't believe we're doing this,' says Mrs. Karimov, smiling at the camera. 'Our house never looks this exciting.'

words.context: 'We're renovating the kitchen and the bathroom.'
Two designers arrive with big plans.
They're a little nervous.
One worker is knocking down an old wall.

grammar_topic: past simple; past continuous
title: The Power Cut
body: Last Tuesday, the whole neighbourhood lost electricity at exactly eight o'clock. Malika was cooking dinner when the lights suddenly went out. She lit two candles and continued chopping vegetables in the dark kitchen. Meanwhile, her neighbours were sitting outside, talking and laughing under the stars. Her brother, who was studying for an exam, complained loudly about his laptop battery. 'I finished my homework just in time,' he said, closing the lid. The power stayed off for almost three hours. While they waited, the family played cards by candlelight, something they hadn't done in years. Malika finally served dinner at half past ten, much later than usual. 'At least the food didn't get cold,' she joked, since the stove used gas, not electricity. When the lights finally came back on, nobody rushed to turn on the television. They just sat there for a moment, blinking in the sudden brightness, strangely sorry that the evening was over.

words.context: Last Tuesday, the whole neighbourhood lost electricity.
She lit two candles.
Her brother complained loudly about his laptop battery.
His laptop battery.
...blinking in the sudden brightness.
Blinking in the sudden brightness.

grammar_topic: past simple; time sequencers and connectors
title: The Longest Bus Ride
body: First, the bus left the station twenty minutes late. Then, after only an hour, it stopped at the side of the road with a flat tyre. While the driver changed the wheel, all the passengers got out to stretch their legs. Suddenly, it started raining, so everyone ran back inside. Afterwards, the bus continued for two more hours until it reached a small town for a break. Farrukh bought bread and tea at a roadside stall before the driver called everyone back. Eventually, as the sun began to set, the bus climbed into the mountains, and the road became narrow and winding. Finally, just before midnight, the bus arrived at the final stop, six hours later than planned. Despite the delay, Farrukh didn't feel angry. Instead, he felt strangely proud, as if he had survived a small adventure. As soon as he stepped off the bus, his cousin ran over and hugged him. 'You made it!' she laughed. 'Next time, take the train.'

words.context: It stopped with a flat tyre.
...to stretch their legs.
Farrukh bought bread and tea at a roadside stall.
The road became narrow and winding.

grammar_topic: be going to; present continuous (future arrangements)
title: The Wedding Plan
body: Nigora is getting married in June, and she's already planning every detail. 'We're having the ceremony in my grandmother's garden,' she tells her friend, showing photos on her phone. 'And my cousin is bringing the flowers from her shop.' She's going to wear her mother's old wedding dress, which a tailor is currently altering. Her fiancé, Bekzod, isn't worried about the details; he's simply going to trust Nigora's plans completely. 'I'm meeting the photographer on Thursday,' Nigora continues, 'and we're choosing the menu with the restaurant next week.' Her friend asks if she's nervous. 'A little,' Nigora admits, 'but mostly I'm excited.' She's going to invite almost two hundred guests, which seems like a lot, but weddings in her family are always huge. Bekzod is picking up the rings tomorrow morning, and after that, there's really nothing left to organize except waiting for June to arrive.

words.context: We're having the ceremony in my grandmother's garden.
A tailor is currently altering it.
A tailor is currently altering the dress.
Her fiancé, Bekzod, isn't worried.
She's going to invite almost two hundred guests.
Nothing left to organize.

grammar_topic: defining relative clauses; be going to
title: The Perfect Flat
body: Jamshed is looking for a flat that's close to his office and doesn't cost too much money. The agent, who has shown him five apartments already, calls with one more option. 'It's a flat that has a small balcony and a kitchen that just got renovated,' she explains. Jamshed, who hates wasting time, agrees to see it immediately. The building, which was built only two years ago, looks modern and clean. Inside, he meets the owner, a woman who works as a teacher nearby. 'This is the room where I keep my books,' she says, showing him around. Jamshed likes the flat that overlooks a quiet street with trees. 'I'm going to think about it tonight,' he tells the agent, though he already knows the answer. The neighbours, who he briefly meets in the hallway, seem friendly enough. By the next morning, Jamshed is going to sign the contract for the flat that finally feels like home.

words.context: The agent calls with one more option.
A flat that has a small balcony.
A kitchen that just got renovated.
The flat overlooks a quiet street.

grammar_topic: present perfect + yet, just, already
title: Not Everything Yet
body: We've just moved into our new apartment, and boxes are still everywhere. 'Have you unpacked the kitchen yet?' my mother asks over the phone. 'I've already finished the kitchen,' I tell her, 'but I haven't touched the bedroom yet.' My brother has already hung the pictures in the living room, though nothing matches on the walls. 'Have you found the coffee machine yet?' he asks, clearly missing his morning coffee. 'Not yet,' I admit, 'it's probably still in one of these boxes.' We've already met one neighbour, an elderly man who has already brought us a plate of biscuits. I haven't seen the whole building yet, but I've already noticed how quiet the street is. My mother asks if we've registered our new address yet. 'We haven't done that yet,' I confess, 'but we'll go tomorrow.' Slowly, box by box, this empty apartment is already starting to feel like ours.

words.context: Have you unpacked the kitchen yet?
My brother has already hung the pictures.
Nothing matches on the walls.
We've already met one neighbour.

'We haven't done that yet,' I confess.

grammar_topic: present perfect or past simple (1); something, anything, nothing
title: Still Waiting to Hear
body: Sitora had her job interview three days ago, but she hasn't heard anything from the company yet. 'Did they say when they'd call?' her flatmate asks. 'They said they'd call by Friday,' Sitora replies, 'but nothing has happened so far.' Yesterday, she checked her email ten times, hoping for something, anything, but there was nothing in her inbox except adverts. She has already applied to two other companies, just in case. Last week, she felt confident after the interview; the manager smiled a lot and asked detailed questions about her experience. Now, she isn't sure if that meant anything at all. Her flatmate has been through this before and has some advice. 'I once waited two whole weeks for an answer,' she says, 'and it turned out fine.' Sitora nods, though it doesn't help much right now. She hasn't told her parents about the interview yet, in case there's nothing to tell. She decides to wait until tomorrow before calling the company herself.

words.context: Her flatmate asks about the interview.
There was nothing in her inbox except adverts.
Nothing except adverts.
The manager asked detailed questions.
She felt confident after the interview.
Her flatmate has some advice.

grammar_topic: comparative adjectives and adverbs; as...as
title: Two Cafés, One Street
body: On the same street, there are two small cafés, and everyone in town has an opinion about them. The café on the corner is cheaper than the one opposite, but its coffee isn't as strong as its rival's. The waiters there are friendlier, though the tables are smaller and closer together. Across the street, the newer café looks more modern, with bigger windows and softer music. Its cakes are more expensive, but customers say they're worth it. 'This coffee is just as good as the one in the capital,' an old man tells his friend, tapping the table proudly. The corner café is busier in the mornings, while the modern one fills up faster in the evenings. Prices there are higher, but the service is quicker. Some people are more loyal to one café than the other, arguing for hours about which is truly better. Personally, I think both cafés are as important to this street as the old clock tower nearby.

words.context: Its coffee isn't as strong as its rival's.
The waiters there are friendlier.
Some people are more loyal to one café.

grammar_topic: superlatives (+ ever + present perfect); quantifiers: too, not enough
title: The Best Meal I've Ever Had
body: 'This is the best meal I've ever eaten in this city,' Dilnoza says, putting down her fork. The restaurant, hidden in a small side street, is the quietest place she's ever found for dinner. 'It's also the cheapest of the three restaurants we've tried this month,' her husband adds. The portions are generous, though some dishes are too spicy for their daughter, who prefers milder food. 'There isn't enough sauce for the rice,' the little girl complains, pushing her plate slightly. The waiter, the most patient one they've ever met, brings extra sauce without being asked twice. 'This is definitely the friendliest restaurant we've visited,' Dilnoza's husband says, looking around at the busy tables. Dilnoza has never had such fresh bread before, still warm from the oven. There isn't enough time to try dessert tonight, but she's already planning her next visit. 'We should come back,' she says. 'This might be the best discovery we've made all year.'

words.context: The portions are generous.
The portions are generous.
Their daughter prefers milder food.
There isn't enough sauce for the rice.

grammar_topic: will / won't (predictions)
title: The Weather Forecaster's Bet
body: Our local weather forecaster, Umar, makes a bold prediction every morning on the radio. 'It won't rain today,' he announces confidently, 'and the sky will stay clear until evening.' His listeners have learned not to trust him completely, since he's often wrong. Today, within an hour, dark clouds appear, and by lunchtime, it's raining heavily. 'This will pass quickly,' Umar insists on air, though the storm continues for the rest of the afternoon. His colleagues joke that if Umar predicts sunshine, everyone should bring an umbrella. 'Tomorrow will definitely be warmer,' he promises the next day, and for once, he's right. The office football team, half-serious, will bet a coffee on his forecasts every Friday. This week, Umar owes three coffees already. 'I won't give up,' he laughs, checking the satellite images again. 'One day, this city will finally trust my forecasts.' Until then, most people will simply carry an umbrella, just in case.

words.context: Our local weather forecaster, Umar.
Makes a bold prediction every morning.

grammar_topic: will / won't / shall (other uses); review of verb forms
title: Shall We Surprise Her?
body: 'Shall we organize a surprise party for grandma's birthday?' Malika asks her brothers. 'I'll book the restaurant,' says the eldest, already reaching for his phone. 'I won't tell her anything, I promise,' laughs the youngest, who usually can't keep a secret. Their grandmother has celebrated many birthdays before, but this year will be different — the whole family is coming, even relatives from abroad. 'Shall I bake the cake, or will you order one?' Malika asks her sister. They decide together: she'll bake it, since grandma always says shop cakes won't taste as good as homemade ones. Yesterday, they walked past a shop, and grandma admired a blue scarf — that will be part of her present. On the day itself, everyone will hide in the garden until she arrives home from her walk. 'Will she really be surprised?' the youngest asks nervously. 'She's suspected nothing so far,' Malika reassures him. Soon, the whole family will shout 'Surprise!' together, and grandma won't stop smiling all evening.

words.context: A surprise party for grandma's birthday.

Even relatives from abroad.

grammar_topic: uses of the infinitive with to; uses of the gerund (verb + -ing)
title: Trying to Change
body: Every January, Rustam decides to change something about his life. This year, he's chosen to stop eating sugar and to start running every morning. He remembers avoiding exercise for years, always finding an excuse not to go. 'I enjoy sleeping more than jogging,' he used to joke with his colleagues. But after visiting the doctor, he agreed to try a healthier routine. Waking up early was the hardest part; he kept forgetting to set his alarm properly. Slowly, he managed to build a habit, and running became less painful. He also decided to stop drinking coffee after six in the evening, hoping to sleep better. His wife suggested cooking dinner together instead of ordering food, so they started preparing meals every night. By March, Rustam had learned to enjoy running, something he never expected to happen. 'I don't mind waking up early anymore,' he admits, tying his shoelaces before sunrise. Changing old habits, he realizes, takes more patience than he expected.

words.context: Every January, Rustam decides to change something.

grammar_topic: have to, don't have to, must, mustn't
title: The Exam Room Rules
body: Before the exam starts, the supervisor reads out the rules to the nervous students. 'You must switch off your phones completely,' she says, 'and you mustn't bring any notes into the room.' Students don't have to bring their own pens, since the school provides them, but they have to bring a valid student card. 'You mustn't talk to anyone once the exam begins,' the supervisor warns, walking between the desks. Latecomers don't have to worry too much — they still have to finish at the same time as everyone else, with less time to write. Halfway through, a girl raises her hand; she has to ask for more paper. 'You don't have to raise your hand for that,' the supervisor smiles, 'just walk quietly to my desk.' Students who finish early mustn't leave immediately; they have to wait until the final bell rings. Outside, parents wait nervously, though they know they mustn't enter the building until the exam officially ends.

words.context: The supervisor reads out the rules.
A valid student card.

grammar_topic: should
title: What Should I Do?
body: Farida can't decide whether to change her job, so she calls her older sister for advice. 'You should make a list of the good and bad things about your current job,' her sister suggests. 'You shouldn't decide something this important in one evening.' Farida admits she's been unhappy for months, but she's afraid of starting somewhere new. 'You should talk to your manager first,' her sister continues, 'maybe things can improve without you leaving.' Farida wonders if she should also ask for a higher salary while she's at it. 'You shouldn't be afraid to ask,' her sister laughs, 'the worst answer is just no.' They talk for almost an hour, discussing every possible option. In the end, Farida decides she should try talking to her manager before making any big decision. 'You should call me after the meeting,' her sister says. 'And you shouldn't worry so much beforehand — you always find a solution.'

words.context: She calls her older sister for advice.
Her sister suggests.
You should talk to your manager first.
Ask for a higher salary.

grammar_topic: if + present, will + infinitive (first conditional); possessive pronouns
title: Whose Picnic Is It Anyway?
body: 'If it doesn't rain tomorrow, we'll have the picnic in the park,' Aziza tells her friends. 'If it rains, we'll move everything to my place instead.' Everyone agrees, though nobody wants to carry the heavy basket — it's not mine, someone insists, it's yours, another replies, pointing at a different friend. If the basket is actually his, he'll have to carry it himself. Aziza checks whose blanket they're bringing; hers is too small for six people, so they need a bigger one. 'If Dilshod brings his blanket, we won't need mine at all,' she decides. If everyone arrives on time, they'll catch the best spot near the lake. If someone forgets their food, they'll simply share everyone else's. By the time Saturday arrives, the weather looks perfect, and if nothing changes, the picnic will finally happen exactly as planned — with whichever blanket, and whichever basket, someone remembers to bring.

words.context: Nobody wants to carry the heavy basket.

grammar_topic: if + past, would + infinitive (second conditional)
title: If I Won the Lottery
body: 'If I won the lottery, I would buy a small house by the sea,' Aziz tells his friends during their usual coffee break. 'I wouldn't quit my job completely, though — I'd probably work part-time.' His friend disagrees. 'If I had that much money, I'd stop working immediately and travel for a year.' Someone else jokes that if he became rich suddenly, his relatives would appear from nowhere, asking for loans. 'If I were you, I'd keep it a secret,' Aziz warns, only half joking. They imagine what they would do with the first million: some would help their parents, others would invest in a small business. 'If money weren't a problem, would you still do the same job?' Aziz asks the group. Most admit they wouldn't, though a few say they'd miss the daily routine. By the end of the break, nobody has won anything, but everyone returns to work slightly happier, having spent ten minutes living a different life.

words.context: If I won the lottery.

grammar_topic: present perfect + for and since; present perfect or past simple? (2)
title: Friends Since School
body: Malika and Nodira have known each other since primary school, almost twenty years now. They've lived in different cities for the last five years, but they've stayed close friends since university. 'I haven't seen you properly since your wedding,' Malika says, hugging her old friend at the café. 'I know, I've been so busy since I started the new job,' Nodira replies. They last met in person two years ago, when Nodira visited briefly for a family event. Since then, they've only spoken on video calls, usually late at night. 'Do you remember when we got lost in the old town?' Malika laughs, recalling a trip they took years ago. Nodira has worked at the same company for three years now and finally feels settled. 'I moved to this city last spring,' Malika explains, 'so we're neighbours again, for the first time since school.' They order more tea, in no hurry to end a conversation they've been waiting years to have properly.

words.context: Since primary school, almost twenty years.

grammar_topic: expressing movement (prepositions and verbs); word order of phrasal verbs
title: Across the Finish Line
body: The runners climb over the wooden wall, crawl under the low net, and jump across the muddy pool without stopping. Jahongir runs through the forest path, then splashes straight into the cold river crossing. He climbs up the steep hill, breathing heavily, and slides down the other side on purpose, laughing. Near the end, he has to carry a heavy tyre from one point to another before he can put it down again. His friend, running just behind him, calls out to cheer him on. Jahongir picks up his pace and pushes himself forward across the final field. Volunteers hand out water bottles as runners rush past them towards the finish. He climbs one last rope wall, drops down onto soft sand, and finally crosses the line, exhausted but proud. His friend catches up with him a minute later, and they both sit down to rest. 'I nearly gave up back there,' Jahongir admits, 'but I kept going anyway.'

words.context: Crawl under the low net.

grammar_topic: the passive
title: How Our Bread Is Made
body: Every morning at four o'clock, the bakery on our street is opened by the same two bakers, before anyone else is awake. First, the flour is mixed with water, salt, and yeast in a large metal bowl. The dough is then kneaded by hand for almost twenty minutes until it becomes smooth. Afterwards, it's left to rise for an hour, covered by a thin cloth. Once it has risen, the dough is shaped into round loaves by the older baker, who has done this job for thirty years. Each loaf is then placed carefully into the hot oven, where it's baked for exactly forty minutes. While the bread is being baked, the smell fills the whole street, and customers are already queuing outside. By seven o'clock, the first loaves are taken out and are sold within minutes. 'This bread isn't made with any machines,' the baker tells a curious customer. 'Everything here is still done the old way.'

words.context: The bakery on our street.

grammar_topic: used to
title: Ask the Teacher
body: Mr. Aliyev used to teach maths at our school for almost thirty years, and he still visits every autumn. 'This building used to look completely different,' he tells the current students, pointing at the modern hallway. 'We used to have wooden desks, and there used to be a big tree right where the canteen is now.' Some students find it hard to imagine a school without computers. 'I used to walk two hours to get here every morning,' he continues, smiling at their surprised faces. He used to give extra maths classes on Saturdays, something the school doesn't offer anymore. 'Did you use to enjoy teaching us?' a student asks curiously. 'I used to worry I wasn't strict enough,' he laughs, 'but looking back, I think I was exactly strict enough.' Before he leaves, he reminds them that homework used to be much harder in his day, though nobody quite believes him.

words.context: Right where the canteen is now.

grammar_topic: might; so / neither + auxiliary verbs
title: Neither Do I
body: 'I might go hiking this weekend, if the weather stays good,' Sabina tells her colleague during lunch. 'So might I,' he replies, surprised. 'I don't really enjoy crowded places on weekends,' Sabina admits. 'Neither do I,' he says, laughing at how similar their plans sound. 'I might invite a few friends, but I haven't decided yet.' 'Neither have I,' he replies, 'I might just go alone if nobody's free.' They discover they might both be going to the same mountain trail, at roughly the same time. 'I've never actually hiked that trail before,' Sabina says. 'Neither have I, but I might try the shorter path first.' 'So might I — the longer one might be too difficult for one afternoon.' By the end of lunch, they've quietly arranged to meet at the trail entrance on Saturday morning. 'I might bring a picnic,' Sabina adds. 'So will I,' he laughs. 'Looks like neither of us needs to hike alone this weekend.'

words.context: Sabina tells her colleague during lunch.

grammar_topic: Past Perfect
title: The Meeting That Already Ended
body: By the time Karim arrived at the office, the meeting had already started without him. He had left home early, but a sudden traffic jam had delayed him for almost an hour. When he finally reached the meeting room, everyone had already left; the discussion had finished ten minutes earlier. His manager had sent an email that morning, moving the meeting time, but Karim hadn't checked his phone since breakfast. He realized he had missed an important decision about his own project. His colleague explained that the team had already agreed on a new deadline, one Karim hadn't known about. He felt annoyed that nobody had called him directly. Later, he discovered that his manager had actually tried to call twice, but Karim's phone had been on silent all morning. By lunchtime, Karim had accepted that the mistake was partly his own, and he promised himself he would never leave his phone on silent again.

words.context: A sudden traffic jam had delayed him.

grammar_topic: reported speech; questions without auxiliaries
title: Who Said What?
body: At the family dinner, everyone starts arguing about who said what earlier that day. 'You said you'd finish the shopping,' Malika tells her husband. He replies that he told her he would try, not that he would definitely finish it. Their daughter mentions that grandma had said the soup needed more salt, though grandma insists she said no such thing. 'Who broke the vase in the hallway?' Malika asks, looking around the table. Nobody answers directly; her son says his sister told him it was already broken before he touched it. 'What happened at school today?' Malika asks, trying to change the subject. Her daughter explains that the teacher had asked who wanted to join the choir, and almost everyone raised their hand. 'Who wants dessert?' Malika finally asks, and this time every hand goes up immediately, without a single argument. Later, washing the dishes, Malika smiles, thinking that in this house, someone always says something different from what actually happened.

words.context: Everyone starts arguing.
Their daughter mentions that grandma had said.
Grandma insists she said no such thing.
Who broke the vase in the hallway?
